name: Ben Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate an electric rope shovel at a large open-pit iron ore mine, the kind of machine that's the size of a house and fills a haul truck in four passes. Day shift I'm in the cab by six-thirty, check the dig plan on the screen, then I load trucks for twelve hours with a break when the truck queue runs dry. I like the precision, getting a clean face and a full bucket every time. What wears me out is sitting still for that long, my legs go numb by three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the dig plan on the screen. How much technology is in your cab these days?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More every year, and I'm the one who reads the manuals for fun. I use an AI assistant every day, at home and on my breaks, to check our dig sequence, to understand our pay agreement, even to plan a garden. Nadia, my wife, is a pharmacist, and our two are grown, Karim works in software and Samira's a midwife. We've got good savings and some shares, and we're both on the left, so we argue with the TV about tax at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown, honestly, and I'd post a long thread about why the hype got ahead of the engineering. At work I'd tell the crew that the shovel's not going anywhere. Some would be relieved, some wouldn't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on in the cab and retire at about sixty-three, which was the plan. It also means the tools I use stay useful but small, a better calculator. I'd be a bit sad about that, because I was looking forward to what came next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same job, same plan, keep using the assistant for the dull paperwork. I'd probably push the company to bring in the collision-avoidance software they keep promising, because that's real and it saves lives. And I'd keep a little bit going into the shares every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small sigh. Like a film trailer that was better than the film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you be disappointed by AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little. I'd been hoping these tools would take the boring bits off people and let us work four days a week for the same pay, which was always the promise of machines. If it fizzles, that argument fizzles with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with your savings in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the shares are in a fund, I don't pick winners. If anything I'd be glad I didn't go all in on the AI companies like Karim's friends did.

S0.say: I'd say it's a letdown and post a long thread about why the hype got ahead of the engineering. At work I'd tell the others the shovel isn't going anywhere.
S0.think: He expects to carry on in the cab and retire at about sixty-three as planned. He's a bit sad that the tools stay small, because he was looking forward to what came next.
S0.do: Keeps his job and retirement plan and keeps using the AI assistant for paperwork. Pushes the company for the promised collision-avoidance software and keeps a small monthly amount going into his share fund.
S0.feel: Calm with a small sigh, like a trailer that was better than the film.
S0.quote: Like a film trailer that was better than the film.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is the rare miner who would be disappointed by a plateau. His progressive hope is that machines shorten the working week for the same pay. He uses AI every day but invests cautiously through a fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions to get smart, not scared. Bargain for the gains, shorter hours, training, a share of the savings. I'd be writing that on the union forum and saying it at the shovel crib hut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of it. I'm the one who already likes the screens, so I'd be in the remote operations centre in the city before most people have read the email. What worries me is the guys who've never touched a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the remote shovel trial in the first round, that's where you run the machine from a control room hundreds of kilometres away. I'd start a lunchtime group showing older operators how to use the AI assistant for rosters and pay slips. And I'd push the union delegate to put shorter hours on the table at the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. A bit guilty about being excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your mine is trialling remote operation. Would you go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First in. I've already asked my supervisor twice. The pay's the same and I'd sleep in my own bed every night instead of doing fly-in rosters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said machines should shorten the week. Who would you push to make that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union, mostly, and then whoever's in government. The company won't give it away, they'll say the savings belong to the shareholders. But if a shovel needs one person in a city instead of three on site, someone should ask where the other two salaries went.

S1.say: I'd say this is the moment for unions to get smart, not scared, and bargain for shorter hours, training and a share of the savings. I'd write that on the union forum.
S1.think: He thinks he'd do well, since he already likes screens and would be in the remote operations centre early. His worry is for colleagues who've never touched a tablet.
S1.do: Applies for the first round of the remote shovel trial and starts a lunchtime group teaching older operators to use AI for rosters and pay slips. Pushes the union delegate to put shorter hours on the table at the next agreement.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with a touch of guilt about the excitement.
S1.quote: If a shovel needs one person in a city instead of three on site, someone should ask where the other two salaries went.
S1.fieldNote: He holds two things at once: personal excitement and a political demand that the gains are shared. He is the only one on his crew already asking to join the remote trial. His guilt about being excited is a telling detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest handover of wealth in history, from workers to whoever owns the machines, and we need laws now. A tax on automation, a public dividend, something. I'd be posting it everywhere and turning up wherever the union called a rally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's an early retirement I didn't choose, probably at sixty. I've got the savings, the shares and Nadia's wage, so we'd be fine. The thing that bothers me is that even the remote room goes, so my clever plan to get ahead turns out to be just a slightly later exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Week one I'd run the numbers with the assistant, retire at sixty versus hang on, and I'd likely take a package if it's offered early. I'd join the union campaign for an automation tax and write to every politician who'd read it. And I'd shift a bit of the fund toward the companies building the robots, because if they're eating the economy I'd like a bite back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own table, but it's strange to be out-adapted after being the guy who always adapted first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty when this lands. What happens to your plan to retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's gone. I'd go at sixty with a package, if the union gets a decent one. Three years early, and I'd miss the cab, but I'd rather leave on a good deal than hang on for a worse one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What would you do in the very first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Nadia and the assistant and go through every number we've got. Then ring the union delegate and ask what they're doing, because two years is not enough to organise anything properly. Then call Karim, because software's going to get hit too.

S2.say: I'd say this is the biggest handover of wealth in history, from workers to whoever owns the machines, and we need laws now, like an automation tax or a public dividend.
S2.think: He expects an unchosen early retirement at sixty, and with savings, shares and Nadia's wage they'd be fine. What stings is that even the remote room goes, so his plan to get ahead only buys a slightly later exit.
S2.do: Runs the retirement numbers with his AI assistant in the first week and would take an early package if offered. Joins the union campaign for an automation tax and moves part of his fund toward robot-building companies.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not for his own table but at the strangeness of being out-adapted after always adapting first.
S2.quote: It's strange to be out-adapted after being the guy who always adapted first.
S2.fieldNote: His strong cushion keeps him from real fear, but the fast picture dents his pride as an early adopter. He hedges by investing in the companies he's campaigning to tax, and doesn't see a contradiction. His worry quickly turns to his son's software job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if we start today. Shorter hours, retraining, and a public share of the profits. I'd be in the union's working group, probably running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I get my remote job, a few good years in the control room, and I retire about when I wanted. It's the sweet spot for me, honestly. Others won't be so lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into the remote operations centre in year one and learn the autonomous systems inside out. I'd keep the lunchtime classes going and help the union write its bargaining claim. And I'd put a bit more into the fund each month while I'm still on full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit busy. It feels like a job I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do five years change things for you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easily. I want the robots to exist, I just want everyone to share in them. Owning a little bit is how I make sure I'm not only on the losing side while I fight for the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be investing in robot companies while campaigning to tax them. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to get through the door, two doesn't. In two, the door closes before I've found the handle. In five, I'm in the room and I can help keep it open for a few others.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if we start today, with shorter hours, retraining and a public share of the profits. I'd probably be running the union's working group on it.
S3.think: He sees five years as his sweet spot: a few good years in the remote control room and retirement roughly when he wanted. He knows others won't be so lucky.
S3.do: Moves into the remote operations centre in the first year and learns the autonomous systems inside out. Keeps running lunchtime AI classes, helps write the union's bargaining claim and puts more into his fund while on full pay.
S3.feel: Calm and busy, like a job he knows how to do.
S3.quote: In two, the door closes before I've found the handle.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is the version where his adaptability pays off fully. He is open about investing in robot makers while pushing to tax them. He talks of holding the door open for others, which keeps his politics personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no excuses, governments should have a full plan by 2030. If they don't, vote them out. I'd be saying it at every branch meeting until they made me stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm retired by then, most likely, and doing fine. The robots don't touch me. So this is about what kind of country my grandkids grow up in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a few years in the remote centre, then retire around sixty-three or sixty-four. I'd stay in the union as a retired member and help with campaigns. And I'd keep learning the tools, because I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, almost content. It's the version where we've got time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. Where are you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira's fine, nobody wants a robot delivering their baby, not for a while anyway. Karim I'd tell to learn the part of software that the AI can't do, talking to people and deciding what to build. And I'd tell both of them to join a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Karim and Samira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd be the old guy in the control room teaching the young ones before I go. That's a nice way to finish. I'd like that more than the two-year version where I just get a letter.

S4.say: I'd say ten years means no excuses, and governments should have a full plan by 2030 or be voted out. I'd say it at every branch meeting.
S4.think: He expects to be retired and comfortable before the robots arrive, so they don't touch him. It's about the kind of country his grandchildren grow up in.
S4.do: Works a few years in the remote centre, then retires around sixty-three or sixty-four. Stays in the union as a retired member helping with campaigns, and keeps learning the AI tools for enjoyment.
S4.feel: Calm, almost content, because there's time to get it right.
S4.quote: I'd be the old guy in the control room teaching the young ones before I go.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he imagines a dignified end to his working life as a teacher in the control room. His concern moves to his children and grandchildren and to holding government to account. He contrasts this with just getting a letter in the fast picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but more for the country than for me. What would help is an automation tax that pays a dividend to everyone, plus paid retraining and a shorter working week, so the gains don't all go to the people who own the shovels.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much people like me are already using this stuff. I'm a shovel operator with a trade certificate and I use AI every single day. Don't assume miners are scared of it, some of us are just waiting to see who gets the money.

headlineQuote: Some of us are just waiting to see who gets the money.
portrait: Ben Haddad is a 58-year-old electric rope shovel operator at a large open-pit iron ore mine who uses an AI assistant every day and reads machine manuals for fun. He and his pharmacist wife have good savings and shares, and he argues for unions, shorter hours and taxing automation. In the slower pictures he plans to move first into the remote operations centre and teach others. The two-year AGI picture leaves him financially fine but stung at being out-adapted. With five or ten years he feels calm and busy, investing in robot makers while campaigning for the gains to be shared.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, more for the country than for himself, because there would be no time to organise and the gains would go to the owners.
whatWouldHelp: An automation tax that pays a dividend to everyone, plus paid retraining and a shorter working week.
